theoryAdd.text: The closeness of f_s and f_p follows from the equivalent circuit. At f_p the motional branch is inductive and resonates with C_M, so its effective capacitance is C_s in series with C_M, which is only very slightly smaller than C_s itself. Writing f_p = f_s√(1 + C_s/C_M) and using √(1 + x) ≈ 1 + x/2 for small x gives the simple spacing formula below. Since C_s/C_M is typically 1/200 to 1/1000, the two resonances are only 0.05 to 0.25 percent apart.

Reactance picture: below f_s the crystal is capacitive, at f_s it is a small resistance R, between f_s and f_p its reactance is inductive and rises steeply, at f_p the impedance is maximum, and above f_p it is capacitive again. A parallel-mode circuit such as the Pierce makes the crystal resonate with an external load capacitance C_L, so the actual frequency lies slightly above f_s. The crystal is therefore specified for a particular C_L, and changing C_L pulls the frequency: a smaller C_L raises it towards f_p and a larger C_L lowers it towards f_s.

theoryAdd.plainText: CL = C1·C2/(C1 + C2) + Cstray  (Pierce load capacitance)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1 - resonances and Q of a crystal
Given: L = 0.1 H, C_s = 0.05 pF, R = 100 Ω, C_M = 10 pF
f_s = 1/(2π√(0.1 × 0.05e-12)) = 1/(2π × 7.07e-8) ≈ 2.251 MHz
f_p = f_s√(1 + 0.05/10) = f_s × 1.0025 ≈ 2.256 MHz
f_p − f_s ≈ f_s·C_s/(2C_M) = 2.251e6 × 0.0025 ≈ 5.6 kHz
Q = ω_sL/R = 2π × 2.251e6 × 0.1/100 ≈ 14 100
Compare: a good LC tank has Q of about 100, so the crystal is about 140 times sharper.

Worked example 2 - Pierce clock design
Crystal: 16 MHz, rated C_L = 20 pF, ±25 ppm; board stray about 4 pF
C_L = C/2 + C_stray  ->  C/2 = 20 − 4 = 16 pF  ->  C_1 = C_2 = 32 pF
Tolerance: Δf = 16e6 × 25e-6 = ±400 Hz
Pulling check (C_s = 0.015 pF, C_M = 5 pF):
  f_L − f_s ≈ 16e6 × 0.015/(2 × (5 + 20)) = 4.8 kHz  (300 ppm above f_s)
Wrong C_1, C_2 would shift f by tens of ppm, eating the tolerance budget.

Overtone and series-mode circuits: a crystal vibrates mechanically only at odd multiples of its fundamental thickness-shear mode, so a 20 MHz cut can be used near 60, 100 or 140 MHz. Because the fundamental always has the most loop gain, an overtone oscillator needs an LC tank tuned near the wanted overtone to kill gain at the fundamental. In a series-mode oscillator the crystal sits in the feedback path, where its minimum impedance at f_s lets feedback through only at that frequency. In the Miller oscillator the crystal is between gate and ground and the drain tank is tuned slightly above the crystal frequency so that it looks inductive; feedback is through the gate-drain capacitance.

items: Placing f_p below f_s; it is always slightly above.
Forgetting the square root in f_p = f_s√(1 + C_s/C_M), which doubles the spacing.
Assuming overtones can be even harmonics; only odd overtones exist.
Treating ppm as percent: 1 ppm = 10^-6 = 0.0001 percent.
Adding the two Pierce capacitors; they are in series across the crystal, plus stray.

theoryAdd.text: The watch crystal frequency 32.768 kHz equals 2^15 Hz, so a chain of 15 divide-by-2 flip-flops gives exactly 1 Hz. A ppm error translates directly into time error: 1 ppm is about 0.0864 s per day.

questions.questionText: A quartz crystal has motional inductance L = 0.5 H and motional capacitance C_s = 0.02 pF. Its series resonant frequency is approximately:
A crystal has L = 0.5 H, C_s = 0.02 pF and mounting capacitance C_M = 5 pF. The parallel resonant frequency exceeds the series resonant frequency by about:
questions.explanation: f_s = 1/(2π√(0.5 × 0.02 × 10^-12)) ≈ 1.5915 MHz and f_p = f_s√(1 + 0.02/5) = f_s√1.004 ≈ 1.5947 MHz, so f_p − f_s ≈ f_sC_s/(2C_M) ≈ 3.18 kHz. Forgetting the square root gives 6.37 kHz.

questions.questionText: A crystal has L = 0.5 H and motional resistance R = 100 Ω, and its series resonant frequency is 1.59 MHz. Its Q factor is about:
questions.explanation: Q = ω_sL/R = (2π × 1.59 × 10^6 × 0.5)/100 ≈ 50 000. Leaving out the 2π gives about 7 960.

questions.questionText: A 4 MHz crystal has motional capacitance C_s = 0.04 pF and motional resistance R = 50 Ω. Its Q is approximately:
A digital watch uses a 32.768 kHz crystal whose frequency is 20 ppm high. The time the watch gains in one day (86 400 s) is about:
questions.explanation: The watch runs fast by the same fraction as its crystal: 86 400 × 20 × 10^-6 ≈ 1.73 s per day. The 0.66 figure is the frequency error in hertz (32 768 × 20 × 10^-6), not a time.

questions.questionText: A 16 MHz microcontroller crystal is rated at ±30 ppm. The maximum deviation from 16 MHz is:
A 25 MHz crystal oscillator is measured at 25.000125 MHz. Its frequency error is:
questions.explanation: Error = (125 Hz/25 × 10^6 Hz) × 10^6 = 5 ppm high.

questions.questionText: A 10 MHz crystal oscillator has a temperature coefficient of 1 ppm/°C over its operating range (assume linear). If its temperature rises by 30 °C, the frequency changes by about:
questions.explanation: Total drift = 1 ppm/°C × 30 °C = 30 ppm, so Δf = 10 × 10^6 × 30 × 10^-6 = 300 Hz.

questions.questionText: A crystal with a fundamental frequency of 20 MHz is operated on its third overtone. The oscillator frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: Overtones are odd mechanical modes, so the third overtone is close to 3 × 20 = 60 MHz (in practice slightly off an exact multiple).

questions.questionText: The fundamental frequency of an AT-cut quartz plate is approximately f = 1.66/t MHz, with the thickness t in millimetres. The thickness needed for a 10 MHz fundamental is about:
questions.explanation: t = 1.66/f = 1.66/10 ≈ 0.166 mm. Frequency is inversely proportional to thickness, which is why high-frequency fundamental plates become fragile.

questions.questionText: A 5 MHz crystal has C_s = 0.025 pF and C_M = 6.25 pF. By what percentage does f_p exceed f_s?
questions.explanation: f_p/f_s = √(1 + C_s/C_M) = √1.004 ≈ 1.002, so f_p is about 0.2 % (about 10 kHz) above f_s. The 0.4 % figure forgets the square root.

questions.questionText: A crystal has f_s = 1.000 MHz, f_p = 1.002 MHz and motional capacitance C_s = 0.02 pF. Its mounting capacitance C_M is about:
questions.explanation: (f_p/f_s)² = 1 + C_s/C_M, so C_s/C_M = 1.002² − 1 ≈ 0.004 and C_M = 0.02/0.004 ≈ 5 pF. Using f_p/f_s = 1 + C_s/C_M without squaring gives 10 pF.

questions.questionText: A 10 MHz crystal has motional capacitance C_s = 0.01 pF. Its motional inductance is about:
In a Pierce (CMOS inverter) crystal oscillator the two load capacitors are 33 pF each and the stray capacitance is estimated at 5 pF. The load capacitance seen by the crystal is about:
questions.explanation: The two capacitors are effectively in series across the crystal: C_L = C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2) + C_stray = 16.5 + 5 = 21.5 pF.

questions.questionText: A crystal is specified for a load capacitance of 18 pF. In a Pierce circuit with 3 pF of stray capacitance and two equal load capacitors, each capacitor should be:
questions.explanation: C_L = C/2 + C_stray, so C/2 = 18 − 3 = 15 pF and C = 30 pF. Ignoring the stray capacitance would give 36 pF.

questions.questionText: A 10 MHz crystal (C_s = 0.02 pF, C_M = 5 pF) operates with a load capacitance C_L = 15 pF. Using f_L ≈ f_s[1 + C_s/(2(C_M + C_L))], the oscillation frequency lies above f_s by about:
questions.explanation: Δf = f_sC_s/(2(C_M + C_L)) = 10 × 10^6 × 0.02/(2 × 20) = 5 kHz, a pull of 500 ppm. Leaving out C_M gives 6.7 kHz and dropping the factor 2 gives 10 kHz.

questions.questionText: A 10 MHz crystal resonator has Q = 100 000. Its resonance bandwidth (f/Q) is:
questions.explanation: BW = f/Q = 10 × 10^6/10^5 = 100 Hz, an extremely narrow resonance compared with an LC tank.

questions.questionText: A digital watch divides its 32.768 kHz crystal frequency down to 1 Hz with a chain of divide-by-2 flip-flops. The number of flip-flops needed is:
questions.explanation: 32 768 = 2^15, so 15 cascaded divide-by-2 stages give exactly 1 Hz, which is why this frequency is used for watch crystals.

questions.questionText: The piezoelectric effect is the property by which a crystal:
options: Develops a voltage when mechanically stressed, and deforms when a voltage is applied
Conducts current in one direction only
Changes its resistance in a magnetic field
questions.explanation: Piezoelectric materials convert mechanical stress into voltage and voltage into strain; this two-way coupling lets a quartz plate act as an electrical resonator.

questions.questionText: Quartz is preferred for oscillator crystals mainly because it:
options: Is mechanically strong, chemically stable and has a very small temperature coefficient
Has the strongest piezoelectric effect of all materials
Can be tuned over a wide frequency range
questions.explanation: Rochelle salt shows a stronger piezoelectric effect, but quartz is chosen for its strength, stability and low temperature coefficient.

questions.questionText: In the electrical equivalent circuit of a quartz crystal, the motional inductance L represents:
options: The frictional losses in the crystal
The mass (inertia) of the vibrating crystal
The capacitance of the electrodes and holder
questions.explanation: In the electro-mechanical analogy L corresponds to mass, C_s to compliance, R to friction, and C_M is the electrode (holder) capacitance.

questions.questionText: At its series resonant frequency f_s, the impedance of a quartz crystal is:
options: Minimum and approximately equal to its motional resistance R
questions.explanation: At f_s the reactances of L and C_s cancel, leaving only R in parallel with the high reactance of C_M, so the impedance is minimum and nearly equal to R.

questions.questionText: At its parallel (anti-resonant) frequency f_p, a quartz crystal presents:
options: A minimum impedance equal to R
A purely capacitive impedance equal to X_CM
questions.explanation: At f_p the inductive motional branch resonates with C_M, forming a parallel resonance with maximum impedance.

questions.questionText: Between its series and parallel resonant frequencies, a quartz crystal behaves as:
options: A pure resistance of zero ohms
questions.explanation: Above f_s the motional branch is inductive, and up to f_p this inductance dominates, so the crystal acts as a high-Q inductor in this narrow band.

questions.questionText: At frequencies well below f_s, the reactance of a quartz crystal is:
questions.explanation: Below f_s the motional branch is dominated by C_s, and in parallel with C_M the whole crystal is capacitive.

questions.questionText: The main reason a crystal oscillator has far better frequency stability than an LC oscillator is:
options: The extremely high Q of the quartz resonator
questions.explanation: A Q of 10^4 to 10^6 makes the crystal's phase change very steeply with frequency, so circuit changes shift the frequency only minutely.

questions.questionText: The Pierce oscillator is essentially:
options: A Hartley oscillator with a crystal in place of the capacitor
An RC phase-shift oscillator with a crystal in each section
A Wien bridge oscillator with a crystal in the bridge
A Colpitts oscillator with a crystal in place of the inductor
questions.explanation: The Pierce keeps the two-capacitor divider of the Colpitts and uses the crystal, operated where it is inductive, as the tank inductor.

questions.questionText: In a CMOS-inverter Pierce oscillator, a large resistor (about 1 MΩ) connected between the inverter input and output serves to:
options: Bias the inverter into its linear (high-gain) region
Force the crystal onto its third overtone
Discharge the load capacitors at switch-off
questions.explanation: The feedback resistor sets the DC input equal to the DC output, placing the inverter at the middle of its transfer curve where it acts as a high-gain amplifier.

questions.questionText: In a Pierce oscillator the crystal operates:
options: Exactly at f_s, where it is almost a short circuit
Below f_s, where it is capacitive
Well above f_p, where it is capacitive
Between f_s and f_p, where it is inductive (parallel mode)
questions.explanation: The crystal must supply the inductance of the Colpitts-type tank, and it is inductive only between f_s and f_p.

questions.questionText: In a series-mode crystal oscillator the crystal is placed in the feedback path so that:
options: Feedback is large only at f_p, where the crystal impedance is maximum
Feedback is large only at f_s, where the crystal impedance is minimum
The crystal provides the amplifier gain
The crystal acts only as a DC blocking capacitor
questions.explanation: At f_s the crystal is a low resistance and passes the feedback signal; at any other frequency its high impedance blocks feedback.

questions.questionText: Overtone crystal oscillators operate at:
options: Odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th) of the fundamental mechanical mode
questions.explanation: A thickness-shear plate can vibrate only in odd modes, so overtones exist near 3, 5, 7 ... times the fundamental.

questions.questionText: An overtone crystal oscillator needs an LC tank tuned near the desired overtone because:
options: The crystal cannot vibrate without an external inductor
Otherwise the crystal would oscillate on its fundamental, which has the most loop gain
The tank sets the frequency exactly, making the crystal unnecessary
It converts the output to a square wave
questions.explanation: The tank removes gain at the fundamental and lower overtones, so the loop conditions are met only near the chosen overtone while the crystal still fixes the exact frequency.

questions.questionText: Fundamental-mode quartz crystals are rarely made above about 30 MHz because:
options: Quartz loses its piezoelectric property above 30 MHz
The plate would have to be so thin that it becomes fragile and hard to make
questions.explanation: Frequency is inversely proportional to plate thickness, so very high fundamentals need plates only tens of micrometres thick; overtone operation is used instead.

questions.questionText: The main limitation of a crystal oscillator compared with an LC oscillator is that:
options: Its frequency cannot be varied over a wide range
It needs a very large inductor
questions.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the crystal's dimensions; external capacitance can pull it only by a small number of ppm.

questions.questionText: In a VCXO (voltage-controlled crystal oscillator) the frequency is varied by:
options: A varactor diode that changes the load capacitance, pulling the frequency by only tens to hundreds of ppm
Varying the supply voltage to double the frequency
questions.explanation: The varactor alters C_L, and since the crystal is inductive only between f_s and f_p the achievable pull is very small.

questions.questionText: Of the following, the crystal oscillator type with the best frequency stability is the:
questions.explanation: Keeping the crystal at a constant elevated temperature in an oven gives stability of about 0.01 ppm or better, ahead of a TCXO (about ±1 ppm).

questions.questionText: The AT-cut is the most popular quartz cut for MHz-range crystals because:
options: It gives the strongest piezoelectric voltage
Its frequency changes very little with temperature over a wide range around room temperature
questions.explanation: The AT-cut has a cubic frequency-temperature curve that is nearly flat around room temperature, giving a low temperature coefficient.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a typical application of crystal oscillators?
options: A variable-frequency audio tone generator tuned from 20 Hz to 20 kHz
Local oscillator in a GPS receiver
questions.explanation: Crystal oscillators are fixed-frequency references; a widely tunable audio generator uses an RC oscillator such as the Wien bridge.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a crystal oscillator is correct?
options: The crystal generates oscillations by itself without any amplifier
The crystal only sets the frequency; an amplifier is still needed to provide gain and satisfy the Barkhausen criterion
The crystal should be driven at the highest possible power
The crystal can be tuned over an octave with a trimmer capacitor
questions.explanation: The crystal is a passive, high-Q frequency-determining element; the transistor or gate supplies the energy lost in its resistance.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a quartz crystal is NOT correct?
options: Its parallel resonant frequency f_p is lower than its series resonant frequency f_s
Its motional capacitance C_s is much smaller than its mounting capacitance C_M
Its Q is typically 10^4 or more
Its impedance is minimum at f_s
questions.explanation: f_p = f_s√(1 + C_s/C_M) is always slightly higher than f_s; the other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: In a Pierce oscillator the external load capacitance across the crystal is reduced slightly. The frequency of oscillation:
questions.explanation: From f_L ≈ f_s[1 + C_s/(2(C_M + C_L))], a smaller C_L increases the fraction, so the frequency rises towards f_p.

questions.questionText: The series and parallel resonant frequencies of a quartz crystal lie very close together because:
options: The motional inductance is very small
The motional capacitance C_s is very much smaller than the mounting capacitance C_M
The motional resistance is very large
questions.explanation: f_p/f_s = √(1 + C_s/C_M); with C_s/C_M of the order of 0.001 to 0.005 the ratio is only just above 1.

questions.questionText: The very high Q of a quartz crystal results from:
options: The high gain of the amplifier
Its very large L/C_s ratio together with a small motional resistance
questions.explanation: Q = (1/R)√(L/C_s); a large L (henries or millihenries) with a tiny C_s (hundredths of a pF) and modest R gives Q of 10^4 to 10^6.

questions.questionText: In a Miller crystal oscillator the crystal is connected between gate and ground and the drain has a parallel LC tank. For oscillation, the drain tank must be tuned:
options: Exactly to the third harmonic of the crystal
Well below the crystal frequency, so that it is capacitive
Slightly above the crystal frequency, so that it is inductive, with feedback through the gate-drain capacitance
To any frequency, since the tank plays no part
questions.explanation: A parallel tank is inductive below its own resonance, so tuning it slightly above the crystal frequency makes it inductive at the operating point; with the inductive crystal and C_gd this satisfies the phase condition.

questions.questionText: A crystal with a 10 MHz fundamental is used in overtone oscillators. Which of these frequencies is NOT an available overtone?
questions.explanation: Only odd overtones exist (about 30, 50, 70 MHz for a 10 MHz cut); 20 MHz would be an even multiple.

questions.questionText: Driving a quartz crystal with excessive power is likely to:
options: Convert it into an ordinary LC tank
Cause frequency drift and faster ageing, and may even fracture the crystal
questions.explanation: Crystals have a maximum drive level of a few milliwatts or less; overdriving heats and stresses the plate, shifting the frequency and possibly cracking it.
